accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding the applicability of Fundamental Rights:
1. Articles 23 and 24 are denied to all foreigners.
2. Enemy aliens do not enjoy the safeguards under Article 22 in the circumstances specified in Article 22(3).
3. Companies can claim rights available to all persons, but cannot claim the rights under Article 19.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statement 1 is false because Articles 23 and 24 are not denied to aliens. Statements 2 and 3 are correct: Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens from specified safeguards, and companies may claim all-persons rights but not Article 19 rights.
accepted.tq: Find the swapped pair: Articles 23 and 24 are not among the rights denied to aliens.
accepted.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

accepted.s: A foreign national ordinarily residing in India seeks protection against discrimination based solely on place of birth under Article 15. Which of the following is the most appropriate constitutional position?
o: The protection is available because Article 15 is available to every person.
The protection under Article 15 is available only to citizens.
The protection is available only if the person is an enemy alien.
The protection is available only through Article 23.
accepted.x: Article 15 is among the Fundamental Rights available only to citizens. It is not an all-persons right available to foreign nationals merely because they reside in India.
accepted.tq: Apply the citizen-only list to a short factual situation rather than recalling the list mechanically.
accepted.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

accepted.s: Which one of the following Articles is available to both citizens and foreigners, subject to constitutional exceptions?
accepted.x: Article 21 is available to all persons. Articles 19, 16 and 29 are included among the rights available only to citizens.
accepted.tq: Discriminate between the closely placed citizen-only Articles 16, 19 and 29 and the all-persons Article 21.
accepted.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 15
b. Article 20
c. Article 29
d. Article 27

List-II (Availability)
i. Only citizens
ii. All persons
iii. Only citizens
iv. All persons

option codes:
accepted.x: Articles 15 and 29 are available only to citizens, while Articles 20 and 27 are available to all persons. Therefore, the matching is a–i, b–ii, c–iii and d–iv.
accepted.tq: Start from the sure pairs: Article 15 is citizen-only and Article 20 is an all-persons right.
accepted.sec: Rights available only to citizens vs to all persons (Articles 14-30)

accepted.s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Article 23 — Right to freedom of religion
Article 14 — Equality before law and equal protection of laws
accepted.x: Article 23 deals with the right against exploitation, including prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour. The right to freedom of religion is covered by Articles 25 to 28.
accepted.tq: Find the wrong group–article association by checking the standard six-group classification.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s: Part III of the Constitution of India extends from:
accepted.x: Part III contains Fundamental Rights and extends from Article 12 to Article 35.
accepted.tq: Test the exact constitutional range directly, with neighbouring Parts as plausible distractors.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s:
Arrange the following groups of Fundamental Rights in the order in which their article ranges occur in Part III, beginning with the earliest:
A. Right against exploitation
B. Right to equality
C. Cultural and educational rights
D. Right to freedom of religion
accepted.x: The sequence is right to equality (Articles 14–18), right against exploitation (23–24), right to freedom of religion (25–28), and cultural and educational rights (29–30).
accepted.tq: Use the first and last article ranges to place the groups in sequence.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the present number and original number of groups of Fundamental Rights?
accepted.x: The Constitution originally contained seven groups of Fundamental Rights. The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment, leaving six groups at present.
accepted.tq: Separate the original and present figures before examining the options.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s: The right to property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment Act of 1978 and is presently protected as a legal or constitutional right under:
accepted.x: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed Article 31 from the Fundamental Rights chapter. Property is now protected under Article 300A in Part XII as a constitutional/legal right.
accepted.tq: Use the amendment–article–Part chain instead of confusing the former Article 31 with the present provision.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right expressly included in Part III?
o: Right to education for children aged six to fourteen years
accepted.x: The right to employment is a Directive Principle under Article 41, not a Fundamental Right. Education for children aged six to fourteen is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
accepted.tq: Distinguish claimed socio-economic rights from rights expressly placed in Part III.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s:
Consider the following pairs:
1. Equal pay for equal work — Article 39(d)
2. Right to vote — Article 326 and election laws
3. Right to shelter — Express Fundamental Right in Part III
4. Right to property — Article 300A
Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
accepted.x: Pairs 1, 2 and 4 are correct. Equal pay for equal work is a constitutional goal under Article 39(d), voting is a statutory right connected with Article 326 and election laws, and property is protected under Article 300A. Right to shelter is not an express Fundamental Right, though courts have read it into Article 21.
accepted.tq: Check whether each claimed right is express, derivative, statutory or a Directive Principle.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s: The right to education for children between six and fourteen years is a Fundamental Right under:
o: Article 30, inserted by the 73rd Amendment Act
Article 19, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act
Article 24, inserted by the 44th Amendment Act
Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002
accepted.x: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002, making education for children aged six to fourteen a Fundamental Right. The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009 gives effect to it.
accepted.tq: Link the age range, Article 21A and the 86th Amendment without confusing them with child-labour provisions.
accepted.sec: Fundamental Rights - six groups, article range, original vs present number, claimed rights not in Part III

accepted.s: Which of the following statements regarding Fundamental Rights is correct?
o: They can be enforced only after Parliament passes a law under Article 35.
They are enforceable only by the High Courts.
They are non-justiciable because they are political principles.
An aggrieved person may directly approach the Supreme Court under Article 32.
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights are justiciable, and Article 32 permits an aggrieved person to move the Supreme Court directly for their enforcement. High Courts can also enforce them under Article 226, along with other legal rights.
accepted.tq: Identify the constitutional remedy that directly establishes justiciability: Article 32.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements:
1. Fundamental Rights are subject to reasonable restrictions where the Constitution permits such restrictions.
2. Courts examine the reasonableness of restrictions through judicial review.
3. Every Fundamental Right is absolute and cannot be regulated by law.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Fundamental Rights are qualified rather than absolute, and courts review restrictions for constitutional validity and reasonableness. Statement 3 is false.
accepted.tq: Reject the absolute claim and retain the two statements describing the restriction-and-review framework.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: How many grounds of reasonable restriction are listed in Article 19 in all?
accepted.x: Article 19 contains eleven grounds of reasonable restriction in all. These restrictions must be imposed by law and must fall within constitutionally recognised grounds.
accepted.tq: Test the precise numerical detail with nearby figures as distractors.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: Which one of the following is a negative right, in the sense that it primarily limits State action?
accepted.x: Article 20 is a negative right that limits State action in relation to conviction for offences. Articles 21A, 29 and 30 are examples of positive rights conferring particular privileges or protections.
accepted.tq: Distinguish negative restraints on the State from positive rights that confer privileges.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: Which one of the following sets consists only of examples of positive Fundamental Rights?
accepted.x: Articles 21A, 29 and 30 confer educational or cultural privileges and are treated as examples of positive rights. The other sets contain negative rights that primarily restrict State action.
accepted.tq: Classify each option by the direction of the right rather than by its subject title.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: Which one of the following Articles is NOT included among the provisions imposing near-absolute limits on legislative power?
accepted.x: Articles 15, 17, 18, 20 and 24 are identified as provisions imposing near-absolute limits on legislative power. Article 19 permits reasonable restrictions on specified grounds and is therefore not in that group.
accepted.tq: Find the exception within a closely related Article list.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: Fundamental Rights are primarily enforceable against the State, but which of the following Articles also operate against private persons in the situations covered by them?
accepted.x: Although most Fundamental Rights operate against State action, Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 also impose obligations relevant to private persons. The other combinations do not represent the specified group.
accepted.tq: Use the exception-to-the-general-rule method: identify the Articles that can bind private persons.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: The model for the Fundamental Rights chapter of the Indian Constitution was principally drawn from the:
accepted.x: The Fundamental Rights chapter of the Indian Constitution was modelled principally on the United States Bill of Rights.
accepted.tq: Test the foreign constitutional source directly, using other constitutional models as distractors.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Fundamental Rights?
o: They are both natural and legal rights and protect individuals as well as minorities.
They are only legal rights and have no natural-rights character.
They protect only minorities and not individuals.
They are exclusively political rights available only during elections.
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights have both natural and legal dimensions and are intended to protect individuals and minorities. They are not confined to electoral or exclusively political rights.
accepted.tq: Choose the comprehensive description and reject options that use exclusive language.
accepted.sec: Features of Part III - justiciable, not absolute, reasonable restrictions, positive vs negative, foreign model

accepted.s: Which authority alone is empowered under Article 33 to restrict the application of Fundamental Rights to members of the armed forces and specified security services?
o: The Supreme Court by judicial order
accepted.x: Article 33 empowers Parliament alone to restrict or abrogate the application of Fundamental Rights for members of the armed forces, paramilitary forces, police, intelligence organisations and related staff, including specified non-combatants.
accepted.tq: Ask who would do this job: Article 33 expressly assigns the power to Parliament, not the executive or States.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

accepted.s:
Consider the following statements regarding Article 33:
1. Parliament may restrict Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces.
2. The power may extend to specified non-combatant employees such as cooks and barbers.
3. State Legislatures may exercise the same power independently for maintaining public order.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
accepted.x: Statements 1 and 2 are correct. Article 33 gives the power exclusively to Parliament, so Statement 3 is false.
accepted.tq: Spot the wrong authority in Statement 3 while retaining the specific scope of Article 33.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

accepted.s: Which one of the following statements regarding Article 34 is correct?
o: It automatically suspends Articles 20 and 21 whenever martial law is declared.
It deals with preventive detention during a National Emergency only.
It empowers State Legislatures to declare martial law throughout India.
It permits restriction of Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force and allows Parliament to indemnify officials; martial law is not defined in the Constitution.
accepted.x: Article 34 concerns restrictions on Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force and permits Parliament to indemnify officials for acts connected with it. The Constitution does not define martial law.
accepted.tq: Combine the Article 34 subject, Parliament’s indemnity power and the constitutional omission on definition.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

accepted.s: Under Article 35, which body has exclusive legislative competence to make laws on the matters specified in that Article?
accepted.x: Article 35 assigns legislative power exclusively to Parliament for matters including Articles 16(3), 32(3), 33 and 34, and for prescribing punishments for offences under Part III. The purpose is uniformity throughout India.
accepted.tq: Apply the exclusive-authority trap to distinguish Parliament from State Legislatures.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

accepted.s:
Match List-I with List-II and select the correct answer using the code given below:

List-I (Article)
a. Article 33
b. Article 34
c. Article 35
d. Article 359

List-II (Provision)
i. Restriction during martial law and indemnity by Parliament
ii. President’s order suspending enforcement of specified Fundamental Rights
iii. Parliament’s exclusive power to legislate on specified Part III matters
iv. Restriction of Fundamental Rights of specified forces and security services

option codes:
accepted.x: Article 33 concerns specified forces and security services, Article 34 concerns martial law, Article 35 gives Parliament exclusive legislative power on specified matters, and Article 359 concerns the President’s order suspending enforcement of named rights.
accepted.tq: Start with the distinctive pairs Article 33–forces and Article 34–martial law, then complete the remaining matches.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

accepted.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 358 and 359?
o: Article 358 operates only during armed rebellion, whereas Article 359 operates only during financial emergency.
Article 358 concerns automatic suspension of Article 19 during war or external aggression, whereas Article 359 concerns a Presidential order suspending enforcement of named Fundamental Rights.
Article 358 is a power of the Supreme Court, whereas Article 359 is a power of Parliament.
Article 358 suspends enforcement of all Fundamental Rights, whereas Article 359 suspends only Article 19.
accepted.x: Article 358 automatically suspends Article 19 only when the Emergency is based on war or external aggression, not armed rebellion. Article 359 enables the President to suspend enforcement of named Fundamental Rights by order, but not Articles 20 and 21.
accepted.tq: Split the two similar provisions by authority, trigger and scope instead of treating both as identical emergency powers.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

accepted.s: A constitutional amendment affecting a Fundamental Right is challenged before the Supreme Court. Which of the following principles is applicable?
o: Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances.
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights only through a constitutional amendment, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights through an ordinary statute without limitation.
Only State Legislatures may amend Fundamental Rights.
accepted.x: Fundamental Rights may be altered through the constitutional amendment procedure, but the amendment is subject to the basic-structure doctrine laid down in Kesavananda Bharati (1973). An ordinary law cannot amend the Constitution.
accepted.tq: Distinguish constitutional amendment from ordinary legislation and apply the basic-structure limitation.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35

accepted.s: The basic-structure limitation on Parliament’s amending power is associated with which case and year?
accepted.x: The basic-structure doctrine was laid down in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala in 1973. It limits Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution, including provisions relating to Fundamental Rights.
accepted.tq: Link the doctrine with its leading case and year, while avoiding nearby constitutional cases.
accepted.sec: Who can limit Fundamental Rights - Parliament vs courts, Articles 33-35
